children.name: Agelaius
children.description: The red-winged and yellow-winged blackbirds — medium-sized icterids named for their distinctive shoulder patches. Males are black with bold red or yellow epaulets, which they flash aggressively during territorial displays. They are highly polygynous, with dominant males defending territories that attract multiple females, who build nests woven into cattails and marsh vegetation.

children.name: Agelaius phoeniceus
children.description:
The red-winged blackbird (Agelaius phoeniceus) is a passerine bird of the family Icteridae found in most of North America and much of Central America. It breeds from Alaska and Newfoundland south to Florida, the Gulf of Mexico, Mexico, and Guatemala, with isolated populations in western El Salvador, northwestern Honduras, and northwestern Costa Rica. It may winter as far north as Pennsylvania and British Columbia, but northern populations are generally migratory, moving south to Mexico and the Southern United States.
Claims have been made that it is the most abundant living land bird in North America, as bird-counting censuses of wintering red-winged blackbirds sometimes show that loose flocks can number in excess of a million birds per flock and the full number of breeding pairs across North and Central America may exceed 250 million in peak years. It also ranks among the best-studied wild bird species in the world. The red-winged blackbird is sexually dimorphic; the male is all black with a red shoulder and yellow wing bar, while the female is a nondescript dark brown. Seeds and insects make up the bulk of the red-winged blackbird's diet.

children.name: Agelaius humeralis
children.description: The tawny-shouldered blackbird (Agelaius humeralis), known in Spanish as mayito, is a species of bird in the family Icteridae. It is found in Cuba and Hispaniola (split between the Dominican Republic and Haiti). It is a vagrant in the United States (to the Florida Keys).

children.name: Agelaius xanthomus
children.description: The yellow-shouldered blackbird (Agelaius xanthomus), known in Puerto Rican Spanish as mariquita de Puerto Rico or capitán, is a species of blackbird endemic to Puerto Rico. It has black plumage with a prominent yellow patch on the wing. Adult males and females are of similar appearance. The species is predominantly insectivorous.

children.name: Agelaius tricolor
children.description: The tricolored blackbird (Agelaius tricolor) is a passerine bird of the family Icteridae.

children.name: Agelaius assimilis
children.description:
The red-shouldered blackbird (Agelaius assimilis), known in Cuban Spanish as mayito de la ciénaga (swamp mayito) or sargento cubano (Cuban sergeant) and turpial de hombros rojos (red-shouldered troupial), is a species of passerine bird in the family Icteridae endemic to Cuba. It is similar to other species in the genus Agelaius, but recent research has established it as a separate species from the closely related red-winged blackbird (Agelaius phoeniceus).
The males are very similar to those of the red-winged blackbird (Agelaius phoeniceus), while the females are completely black, similar to the males but without the red and yellow stripes on the wings. In addition to having a different behavior, the sexual dimorphism in size and color of the plumage of the red-shouldered blackbird is less than that of the red-winged blackbird.

children.name: Quiscalus
children.description: The grackles — large, glossy blackbirds with long, keeled tails and pale yellow eyes. They are among the most intelligent of all songbirds, capable of solving complex puzzles and remembering individual human faces. Grackles are highly social, forming enormous noisy roosts, and have adapted brilliantly to urban and suburban environments.

children.name: Quiscalus quiscula
children.description: The common grackle (Quiscalus quiscula) is an icterid bird found in large numbers through much of North America.

children.name: Quiscalus mexicanus
children.description:
The great-tailed grackle or Mexican grackle (Quiscalus mexicanus) is a medium-sized, highly social passerine bird native to North and South America. A member of the family Icteridae, it is one of 10 extant species of grackle and is closely related to the boat-tailed grackle and the extinct slender-billed grackle. In the southern and southwestern United States, the grackle is sometimes referred to simply as a "blackbird" or (erroneously) a "crow" due to its glossy black plumage; however, grackles form their own unique genus that is separate from other "blackbirds", such as the red-winged and Brewer's blackbirds, despite being in the same family (Icteridae). Superficially, Brewer's blackbird is one of the most visually similar species to grackles.
In some parts of Mexico, the grackle is sometimes referred to in Spanish as raven ("raven"; "crow"), although it is not a member of the crow genus ( Corvus ) nor of their family ( Corvidae ).

children.name: Quiscalus major
children.description: The boat-tailed grackle (Quiscalus major) is a passerine bird of the family Icteridae found as a permanent resident on the coasts of the Southeastern and Mid-Atlantic United States.

children.name: Quiscalus nicaraguensis
children.description: The Nicaraguan grackle (Quiscalus nicaraguensis) is a species of passerine bird belonging to the genus Quiscalus, a genus of grackles in the New World blackbird family, Icteridae.

children.name: Quiscalus niger
children.description: The Greater Antillean grackle (Quiscalus niger) is a grackle found throughout the Greater Antilles, as well as smaller nearby islands. Like all Quiscalus grackles, it is a rather large, gregarious bird. It lives largely in heavily settled areas.

children.name: Quiscalus lugubris
children.description: The Carib grackle (Quiscalus lugubris) is a New World tropical blackbird, a resident breeder in the Lesser Antilles and northern South America east of the Andes, from Colombia east to Venezuela and northeastern Brazil.

children.name: Molothrus
children.description: The cowbirds — obligate brood parasites that lay their eggs in the nests of other passerine species. They are named for their historical association with bison herds, following the great herds to feed on insects flushed by their movement. A single female may lay several dozen eggs in a season, each in a different host nest, never building a nest or rearing her own young.

children.name: Molothrus ater
children.description: The brown-headed cowbird (Molothrus ater) is a small, obligate brood parasitic icterid native to temperate and subtropical North America. It is a permanent resident in the southern parts of its range; northern birds migrate to the southern United States and Mexico in winter, returning to their summer habitat around March or April.

children.name: Molothrus bonariensis
children.description: The shiny cowbird (Molothrus bonariensis) is a passerine bird in the New World family Icteridae.

children.name: Molothrus rufoaxillaris
children.description: The screaming cowbird (Molothrus rufoaxillaris) is an obligate brood parasite belonging to the family Icteridae and is found in South America.

children.name: Molothrus oryzivorus
children.description: The giant cowbird (Molothrus oryzivorus) is a large passerine bird in the New World family Icteridae.

children.name: Molothrus aeneus
children.description: The bronzed cowbird (Molothrus aeneus), also known as the red-eyed cowbird, is a small icterid native to North America.

children.name: Icterus
children.description: The New World orioles — brilliantly coloured blackbirds with a striking contrast of black and bright yellow, orange, or chestnut. They build remarkable hanging pouch nests woven from plant fibres, suspended from branch tips. Males sing rich, fluty whistles that carry through the treetops. They are primarily frugivorous and insectivorous, and many species undertake long migrations between breeding and wintering grounds.

children.name: Icterus galbula
children.description: The Baltimore oriole (Icterus galbula) is a small icterid blackbird common in eastern North America as a migratory breeding bird.

children.name: Icterus spurius
children.description: The orchard oriole (Icterus spurius) is the smallest species of icterid.

children.name: Icterus chrysocephalus
children.description: | range_map = Icterus chrysocephalus map.svg }}The moriche oriole (Icterus cayanensis chrysocephalus) is a passerine bird in the New World family Icteridae.

children.name: Icterus cayanensis
children.description: | range_map = Icterus cayanensis map 3.svg.

children.name: Icterus pyrrhopterus
children.description: | range_map = Icterus pyrrhopterus map.svg }}.

children.name: Icterus leucopteryx
children.description: | range_map = Icterus leucopteryx map.svg }} The Jamaican oriole (Icterus leucopteryx) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Icterus graduacauda
children.description: Audubon's oriole (Icterus graduacauda), formerly known as the black-headed oriole, is a New World passerine inhabiting the forests and thickets of southeastern Texas and the Mexican coast. It is the only species to have a black hood and yellow body. It is divided into four subspecies and two allopatric breeding ranges. The westernmost range extends from Nayarit south to southern Oaxaca, whereas the eastern range stretches from the lower Rio Grande valley to northern Querétaro. The most common in the western range are the subspecies I. G. Dickeyae and I. G. Nayaritensis; I. G. Graduacauda and I. G. Audubonii can be found in the eastern range. Like most Central American birds, it is not a migratory species and does not display significant sexual dimorphism. DNA analysis of the ND2 and cyt-b genes strongly suggests that I. Graduacauda is most closely related to I. Chrysater, the yellow-backed oriole. It is a member of the genus Icterus and therefore should not be confused with the Old World orioles.

children.name: Icterus pectoralis
children.description:
The spot-breasted oriole (Icterus pectoralis) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.
It is a mid-sized songbird and generally typical oriole. It is bright orange overall with a black bib and black spotting on the sides of the breast. The sexes are similar looking generally but females and juveniles are olive-green on the back and tail, dusky wings, and little or no black on face, throat, or breast. Adults measure in length. Males weigh around on average, while females weigh. The wing bone measures, the tail measures, the culmen measures and the tarsus measures.

children.name: Icterus pustulatus
children.description: The streak-backed oriole (Icterus pustulatus) is a medium-sized species of passerine bird from the icterid family (the same family as many blackbirds, meadowlarks, cowbirds, grackles, and others, including the New World orioles). It is native to Central America and Mexico and is an occasional visitor to the United States.

children.name: Icterus bullockii
children.description: Bullock's oriole (Icterus bullockiorum, also known as Icterus bullockii) is a small New World blackbird. At one time, this species and the Baltimore oriole were considered to be a single species, the northern oriole. This bird is named after William Bullock, an English amateur naturalist.

children.name: Icterus cucullatus
children.description: The hooded oriole (Icterus cucullatus) is a medium-sized New World oriole.

children.name: Icterus gularis
children.description: The Altamira oriole (Icterus gularis) is a New World oriole.

children.name: Icterus parisorum
children.description:
The Scott's oriole (Icterus parisorum) is a medium-sized icterid (the same family as many blackbirds, meadowlarks, cowbirds, grackles, and others, including the New World orioles). The male of this species is bright yellow and black; the female is similar, but with more muted colors.
It is primarily found in the Southwestern United States and south to Baja California Sur and central Mexico. The bird is an infrequent wanderer to eastern North America, with records from New York, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, and Ontario. A bird in New York City's Union Square Park was seen by many in 2007.

children.name: Icterus icterus
children.description: The Venezuelan troupial, known in Venezuela as the Turpial (Icterus icterus), is the national bird of Venezuela.

children.name: Icterus jamacaii
children.description: The campo troupial or campo oriole (Icterus jamacaii) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae that is found in northeastern Brazil.

children.name: Icterus croconotus
children.description:
The orange-backed troupial (Icterus croconotus) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae. It is found in Guyana, Brazil, Paraguay, and eastern Ecuador, Bolivia, and Peru. It is closely related to the Venezuelan troupial (Icterus icterus) and Campo troupial (Icterus jamacaii), and at one time, all three were considered to be the same species.
The term troupial is from French troupiale, from troupe ("troop"), so named because they live in flocks. The Latin name icterus is from Greek ἴκτερος; the icterus was a bird the sight of which was believed to cure jaundice, perhaps the Eurasian golden oriole. It also had the more general meaning "yellow bird", which is why the name was later given to this South American bird. The specific name croconotus literally means "saffron back."

children.name: Icterus abeillei
children.description: The black-backed oriole (Icterus abeillei) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae. It is endemic to Mexico. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical moist lowland forest and subtropical or tropical moist montane forest, but it is also found in cities. It is one of the few species that can consume monarch butterflies due to evolving a tolerance to their natural poison.

children.name: Icterus bonana
children.description: The Martinique oriole (Icterus bonana) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Icterus laudabilis
children.description: The Saint Lucia oriole (Icterus laudablis) is a species of songbird endemic to Saint Lucia. Locally known as the Corouge, it is in the family Icteridae and the genus Icterus (or New World orioles). Due to human development, this species of Oriole (a long with many others in the Caribbean) has seen significant population decline due to invasive species and habitat loss.

children.name: Icterus oberi
children.description: The Montserrat oriole (Icterus oberi) is a medium-sized black-and-yellow icterid (the same family as many blackbirds, meadowlarks, cowbirds, grackles, and others, including the New World orioles).

children.name: Icterus portoricensis
children.description:
The Puerto Rican oriole (Icterus portoricensis), or calandria is a species of bird in the family Icteridae, and genus Icterus or New World blackbirds. This species is a part of a subgroup of orioles (Clade A) that includes the North American orchard oriole, Icterus spurius, and the hooded oriole, Icterus cucullatus.
The Puerto Rican oriole was previously grouped with Cuban oriole (Icterus melanopsis), Hispaniolan oriole (Icterus dominicensis), and Bahama oriole (Icterus northropi) as a single species, (Icterus dominicensis). In 2010, all four species became recognized as full species by the American Ornithologists' Union.

children.name: Icterus dominicensis
children.description: | range_map = Icterus dominicensis map.svg }}.

children.name: Icterus wagleri
children.description:
The black-vented oriole (Icterus wagleri) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae. It is found in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua, and the United States.
Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical dry forest, subtropical or tropical moist lowland forest, and subtropical or tropical moist montane forest.

children.name: Icterus fuertesi
children.description: The orchard oriole (Icterus spurius) is the smallest species of icterid.

children.name: Icterus auratus
children.description: The orange oriole (Icterus auratus) is a small bird species with orange feathers native to the Icteridae family in the Yucatán Peninsula.

children.name: Icterus mesomelas
children.description:
The yellow-tailed oriole (Icterus mesomelas) is a passerine bird in the New World family Icteridae. It breeds from southern Mexico to western Peru and northwestern Venezuela; in Peru it also lives in a river valley corridor.
The yellow-tailed oriole is long and weighs. It is mainly yellow with a black back, lower face and upper breast. The wings are black with yellow epaulets. The tail, seen from above, is black with yellow margins; from below, it appears almost entirely yellow. This is the only oriole with prominent yellow in the tail, hence the species' name. The sexes are similar, but young birds have the black on the back and tail replaced with olive-green.

children.name: Icterus graceannae
children.description:
The white-edged oriole (Icterus graceannae) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae. It is found in Ecuador and Peru.
Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical dry forests and subtropical or tropical moist lowland forests. It is primarily a canopy dweller.

children.name: Icterus maculialatus
children.description:
The bar-winged oriole (Icterus maculialatus) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae. It is found in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Mexico.
Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical moist montane forests and heavily degraded former forest.

children.name: Icterus nigrogularis
children.description: | range_map = Icterus nigrogularis map.svg }}.

children.name: Icterus prosthemelas
children.description:
The black-cowled oriole (Icterus prosthemelas) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae. It is common and widespread in the Caribbean lowlands and foothills from southern Mexico to western Panama. It lives primarily in humid or semihumid forest, as well as in clearings, along forest edges, in plantations, in semi-open areas with scattered trees and bushes, and in gardens. The adult male is black, with yellow on the belly, shoulder, rump, and. The female's plumage varies depending on location. In the south of its range, it is similar to that of the male. In the north, its crown and upperparts are olive-yellow, while its face, throat, upper breast, wings, and tail are black.
It forages mostly at mid-levels, and its diet includes a mix of arthropods, nectar and fruit. The female lays three eggs in a shallow pendent nest, which is stitched to the underside of a large leaf. Both parents defend the nest, and brood and feed the young. Due to its very large range and apparently stable population, it is considered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature to be a species of least concern.

children.name: Icterus chrysater
children.description: The yellow-backed oriole (Icterus chrysater) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Xanthocephalus
children.description: The yellow-headed blackbird — a striking monotypic genus named for the male's vivid yellow head and breast. It breeds in the marshes of western and central North America, often alongside Red-winged Blackbirds. Males defend territories in deep-water cattail marshes and perform impressive flight displays, singing a grating, strained song while hanging from cattail stems.

children.name: Xanthocephalus xanthocephalus
children.description:
The yellow-headed blackbird (Xanthocephalus xanthocephalus) is a medium-sized blackbird with a yellow head.
It is the only member of the genus Xanthocephalus. Their scientific name derives from the Greek word for yellow, xanthous, and the word for head, cephalus.

children.name: Dolichonyx
children.description: The bobolink — a monotypic genus of Grassland icterid with one of the longest migrations of any passerine. The male's breeding plumage is unique among North American birds: black below and on the head, with a buff nape and white back and rump. The species is named for its bubbling, ecstatic song, which pours forth in sustained, tumbling phrases from the male's flight display over hayfields and prairies.

children.name: Dolichonyx oryzivorus
children.description: The bobolink (Dolichonyx oryzivorus) is a small New World blackbird and the only member of the genus Dolichonyx. An old name for this species is the "rice bird", from its tendency to feed on cultivated grains during winter and migration. The bobolink breeds in the summer in the United States and Canada, with most of the summer range in the northern U.S. Bobolinks winter in southern South America, primarily Paraguay, Argentina, and Bolivia. Bobolink numbers are rapidly declining due to factors such as agricultural intensification and habitat loss; they are considered threatened in Canada, and are at risk throughout their range.

children.name: Sturnella
children.description: The meadowlarks — stocky, ground-dwelling icterids with bright yellow underparts and a bold black V on the breast. Despite their name they are not larks but true blackbirds, and are among the most iconic birds of American grasslands. Their clear, fluting songs carry across open fields, and they are more often heard than seen, perching on fence posts and low trees to deliver their melodies.

children.name: Sturnella magna
children.description: The eastern meadowlark (Sturnella magna) is a medium-sized icterid bird, very similar in appearance to its sister species, the western meadowlark.

children.name: Sturnella neglecta
children.description: The western meadowlark (Sturnella neglecta) is a medium-sized icterid bird, about in length.

children.name: Leistes
children.description: A genus of South American meadowlarks separated from Sturnella by genetic evidence, with bright red or yellow underparts and a strong preference for grasslands. Males are highly territorial and perform conspicuous flight displays.

children.name: Leistes loyca
children.description: The long-tailed meadowlark (Leistes loyca) is a passerine bird in the family Icteridae, the oropendolas, New World orioles, and New World blackbirds. It is found in Argentina, Chile, and the Falkland Islands.

children.name: Leistes bellicosus
children.description: The Peruvian meadowlark (Leistes bellicosus) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae, the oropendolas, New World orioles, and New World blackbirds.

children.name: Leistes defilippii
children.description: The Pampas meadowlark (Leistes defilippii) is a Vulnerable species of bird in the family Icteridae, the oropendolas, New World orioles, and New World blackbirds.

children.name: Euphagus
children.description: The American blackbirds — a small genus of two species that bridge the gap between grackles and true blackbirds. They are medium-sized icterids with glossy black plumage, pale eyes, and relatively slender bills. One species is a common bird of towns and farms, while the other has suffered a dramatic and poorly understood population decline.

children.name: Euphagus cyanocephalus
children.description: Brewer's blackbird (Euphagus cyanocephalus) is a medium-sized New World blackbird. It is named after the ornithologist Thomas Mayo Brewer.

children.name: Euphagus carolinus
children.description: The rusty blackbird (Euphagus carolinus) is a medium-sized New World blackbird, closely related to grackles ("rusty grackle" is an older name for the species).

children.name: Cacicus
children.description: The caciques — medium-sized icterids with predominantly black plumage accented by bright yellow, red, or orange patches. They are social birds that build long, hanging pouch nests in colonies, often near wasp nests for protection from predators.

children.name: Cacicus cela
children.description: The yellow-rumped cacique (Cacicus cela) is a passerine bird in the New World family Icteridae. It breeds in much of northern South America from Panama and Trinidad south to Peru, Bolivia and central Brazil. However, they have been sighted as far north as Nayarit state in Mexico.

children.name: Cacicus haemorrhous
children.description:
The red-rumped cacique (Cacicus haemorrhous) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae. It is a species of the Amazon Basin and the Guyanas in northern South America, and is only coastal there in the Guyanas and the Amazon River outlet to the Atlantic; a separate large disjunct range exists in all of south-eastern and coastal Brazil, including Paraguay, and parts of north-eastern Argentina. It is also found in Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, French Guiana, Guyana, Peru, Suriname, and Venezuela.
The red-rumped cacique's natural habitats are subtropical or tropical moist lowland forests, subtropical or tropical swamps, and heavily degraded former forest.

children.name: Cacicus solitarius
children.description: The solitary cacique or solitary black cacique (Cacicus solitarius) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Cacicus koepckeae
children.description: The Selva cacique (Cacicus koepckeae) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Cacicus sclateri
children.description: The Ecuadorian cacique (Cacicus sclateri) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Cacicus chrysonotus
children.description: The mountain cacique (Cacicus chrysonotus) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Cacicus chrysopterus
children.description:
The golden-winged cacique (Cacicus chrysopterus) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae. It is found in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay.
Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical moist lowland forests and subtropical or tropical moist montane forests.

children.name: Psarocolius
children.description: The oropendolas — large icterids with striking combination of black, chestnut, and yellow plumage, and long, pointed bills with colourful tips. They are colonial breeders that weave extraordinary hanging nests up to two metres long, suspended from isolated trees.

children.name: Psarocolius decumanus
children.description: | range_map = Psarocolius decumanus map.svg }}.

children.name: Psarocolius viridis
children.description: The green oropendola (Psarocolius viridis) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Psarocolius angustifrons
children.description: The russet-backed oropendola (Psarocolius angustifrons) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae. It is found in wooded habitats in the highlands of the northern and central Andes and the Venezuelan Coastal Range, and in lowlands of the western Amazon. It is generally common and widespread. Males are larger than females, but otherwise the sexes are similar. Its plumage is mainly olive and brown, and the outer rectrices are contrastingly yellow. The lowland nominate subspecies has a black bill, while the highland subspecies all have pale bills. These have been regarded as separate species, but as they hybridize freely, all major authorities now regard them as a single species. Russet-backed Oropendola JCB.jpg Black billed subspecies in the lowlands of eastern Ecuador Russet-backed oropendolas (Psarocolius angustifrons salmoni) pair grooming Las Tangaras.jpg Pair of P. A. Salmoni, grooming, Colombia

children.name: Psarocolius bifasciatus
children.description: The olive oropendola (Psarocolius bifasciatus) is the largest member of the icterid family and rivals the Amazonian umbrellabird as the largest passerine bird in South America.

children.name: Psarocolius atrovirens
children.description: The dusky-green oropendola (Psarocolius atrovirens) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae (New World blackbirds). It is found on the eastern slope of the Andes in Bolivia and Peru. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical moist montane forests and heavily degraded former forest.

children.name: Psarocolius wagleri
children.description: The chestnut-headed oropendola (Psarocolius wagleri) is a New World tropical icterid bird. The scientific name of the species commemorates Johann Georg Wagler, who established Psarocolius, the oropendola genus.

children.name: Psarocolius montezuma
children.description: The Montezuma oropendola (Psarocolius montezuma) is a New World tropical icterid bird.

children.name: Psarocolius guatimozinus
children.description: The black oropendola (Psarocolius guatimozinus) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae (New World blackbirds).

children.name: Psarocolius cassini
children.description: The Baudó oropendola (Psarocolius cassini) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae. It is endemic to Colombia. Its natural habitat is subtropical or tropical moist lowland forests, which are threatened by destruction. As it is only known from a small number of locations, its conservation status has been assessed as "endangered" by the IUCN.

children.name: Gymnomystax
children.description: The oriole blackbird — a monotypic genus of striking black-and-yellow icterid found in South America. Despite its name, it is not a true oriole but a blackbird with a similar colour pattern.

children.name: Gymnomystax mexicanus
children.description: The oriole blackbird (Gymnomystax mexicanus) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Dives
children.description: A genus of medium-sized, entirely black icterids with a strong, musical song and a preference for open habitats. They are the most thrush-like in appearance among the blackbirds.

children.name: Dives dives
children.description: The melodious blackbird (Dives dives) is a New World tropical bird.

children.name: Dives warczewiczi
children.description: The scrub blackbird (Dives warczewiczi) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Amblycercus holosericeus
children.description: The yellow-billed cacique (Amblycercus holosericeus) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae, the oropendolas, New World orioles, and New World blackbirds. It is found in Mexico, every Central American country, Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Venezuela.

children.name: Chrysomus ruficapillus
children.description: The chestnut-capped blackbird (Chrysomus ruficapillus) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae. It is found in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, French Guiana, Paraguay, and Uruguay, where its natural habitats are swamps, ricefields and pastureland. The International Union for Conservation of Nature rates its conservation status as "least concern".

children.name: Chrysomus icterocephalus
children.description:
The yellow-hooded blackbird (Chrysomus icterocephalus) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae. It is found in grassy and brush areas near water in northern South America, and is generally fairly common. It is sexually dimorphic, and the sexes resemble the respective sexes of the larger yellow-headed blackbird of North America, though the male yellow-hooded blackbird lacks white in the wings.
In 2007, one was found in the Darien Lowlands of Panama. This was a rare vagrant, most likely from Colombia.

children.name: Pseudoleistes guirahuro
children.description: The yellow-rumped marshbird (Pseudoleistes guirahuro) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae. It is a medium-sized bird found in Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay, where its natural habitats are dry savanna, swamps, and pastureland.

children.name: Pseudoleistes virescens
children.description:
The brown-and-yellow marshbird (Pseudoleistes virescens) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.
It is found in the Pampas and north to the Paraguayan border and Rio Grande do Sul, where its natural habitats are swamps and pastureland.

children.name: Nesopsar nigerrimus
children.description: The Jamaican blackbird (Nesopsar nigerrimus) is a species of bird in the New World blackbird and oriole family Icteridae.

children.name: Hypopyrrhus pyrohypogaster
children.description:
The red-bellied grackle (Hypopyrrhus pyrohypogaster) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae. Its genus, Hypopyrrhus, is monotypic.
One of the grackles, it is endemic to Colombia where its natural habitat is subtropical or tropical moist montane forests. The species is threatened by habitat destruction and the International Union for Conservation of Nature considers it to be a "vulnerable species".

children.name: Lampropsar tanagrinus
children.description: The velvet-fronted grackle (Lampropsar tanagrinus) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae, monotypic within the genus Lampropsar. It is found in Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Guyana, Peru, and Venezuela where its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical swamps and heavily degraded former forest.

children.name: Gnorimopsar chopi
children.description: The chopi blackbird (Gnorimopsar chopi) is a species of passerine bird belonging to the family Icteridae, which contains the New World blackbirds, grackles, New World orioles and related species.

children.name: Oreopsar bolivianus

children.name: Agelaioides badius
children.description: The grayish baywing (Agelaioides badius), formerly known as the bay-winged cowbird, is a species of bird in the family Icteridae.

children.name: Amblyramphus holosericeus
children.description:
The scarlet-headed blackbird (Amblyramphus holosericeus) is an icterid found in the South American wetlands.
Scarlet-headed blackbirds occur in pairs in large reed beds in Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay and southern Brazil; Bolivia has an isolated population living at an altitudes of about 600 m. They often perch conspicuously on top of stems. They are uncommon, particularly away from the coast.

children.name: Anumara forbesi
children.description: Forbes's blackbird (Anumara forbesi) is a vulnerable species of New World blackbird that is endemic to the Atlantic forest in South America. This species was named for the British zoologist William Alexander Forbes.

children.name: Xanthopsar flavus
children.description: The saffron-cowled blackbird (Xanthopsar flavus) is a species of bird in the family Icteridae. It is the only species placed in the genus Xanthopsar. It has bright yellow underparts and black or dark brown upperparts. It is found in Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and in Uruguay at the Quebrada de los Cuervos. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical dry lowland grassland, subtropical or tropical seasonally wet or flooded lowland grassland, and pastureland. It is threatened by habitat loss.

children.name: Cercomochus
children.description: Cercomochus — a genus of new world blackbirds.

children.name: Cercomochus nebulosus
children.description: A small, elusive bird with a strikingly patterned plumage. Found in dense forests and wetlands, it has become difficult to study due to its cryptic nature.

children.name: Chrysotheretia
children.description: Chrysotheretia — a genus of new world blackbirds.

children.name: Chrysotheretia garrula
children.description: A vibrant bird with a distinctive yellow throat and black streaks on its breast. They are known for their melodious song, which can be heard throughout the summer.

children.name: Piranga luteola
children.description: A striking bird with a bright yellow throat and upperparts, this species is found in riparian areas and wetlands. Its cheerful song adds to the chorus of spring.

children.name: Halcyon fulva
children.description: This bird is known for its bright yellow throat and upperparts. It is a specialized feeder, often seen in riparian areas.

children.name: Daphoenus
children.description: Daphoenus — a genus of new world blackbirds.

children.name: Daphoenus obscurus
children.description: This tiny bird is a specialist feeder, spending much of its time probing into the leaf litter for insect prey. It has a unique call that can be heard throughout the forest understory.

children.name: Chrysolophus leucophrys
children.description: This unique bird is named for its distinctive song and feeding habits. It is a specialized feeder, often seen flying over wetlands in search of insects.

children.name: Ambrosiceps cassinii
children.description: A small, olive-green bird with a distinctive white eye ring and prominent yellow bill. Found in coastal scrub and wetlands from Nova Scotia to Texas.

children.name: Chlorospingus flavescens
children.description: A small, olive-green bird with a yellow wash on the underparts and distinctive white eye ring. Found in open woodlands from New Mexico to Florida.

children.name: Eurymachus
children.description: Eurymachus — a genus of new world blackbirds.

children.name: Eurymachus eximius
children.description: This warbler has a unique habitat preference, being found only in the cavities of hollow trees. Its striking plumage and song are characteristic features of this species.

children.name: Leptopumachus
children.description: Leptopumachus — a genus of new world blackbirds.

children.name: Leptopumachus lepidus
children.description: Known for its iridescent feathers and melodious song, this species is found in the southern regions of North America. Its bright plumage makes it easily recognizable.

children.name: Terekeca ciliata
children.description: This warbler is known for its crested head and striking plumage. It can often be found in the canopy of mature forests, where it feeds on insects.

children.name: Euphronia canorus
children.description: This bird is known for its distinctive call and overall patterned plumage. It is a specialized feeder, often seen in wetlands.

children.name: Melozone
children.description: Melozone — a genus of new world blackbirds.

children.name: Melozone maculatus
children.description: This waterthrush is named for its spotted plumage. It is a secretive bird, often only glimpsed by those who listen carefully to the sounds of running streams and water.

children.name: Polioptila
children.description: Polioptila — a genus of new world blackbirds.

children.name: Polioptila rufa
children.description: This small warbler is named for its striking black and white plumage. It is a secretive feeder, often seen in dense foliage. Its vocalizations are characteristic of the eastern forests.

children.name: Certhia
children.description: Certhia — a genus of new world blackbirds.

children.name: Certhia melanocephala
children.description: This bird is distinguished by its striking black cap and overall brown plumage. It is a specialized feeder, often seen in coniferous forests.
